feedback: If the learner predicts both become fossils, contrast the two paths: only the buried one is protected from rotting and scavengers.
Reinforce that 'exposed' usually ends in 'no fossil', which is why most animals leave none.
activities.intendedInsight: Burial before decay is the pivotal condition that determines whether anything is preserved at all.
learnerActions: Look at two identical animals that die in the same place; one is buried quickly by sediment, the other is left on the surface.
Predict what will happen to each after a very long time, and say why.
Trace a branching diagram: buried quickly → hard parts remain → minerals replace them → rock → fossil; left exposed → rots/scavenged → no fossil.
Explain in one sentence why quick burial is the step that makes the difference.
activities.title: Compare buried vs exposed: the 'fossil or lost?' branch

feedback: Full response: explains the sequence AND that rapid burial before decay is the crux, that minerals replace the remains over millions of years, and that this is why fossils are rare — transferring to the garden-bone or open-ground counterexample.
Partial response: lists steps (dies, buried, turns to rock) but cannot explain why quick burial matters or why fossils are rare — recites a sequence without the mechanism; prompt for the 'why'.

Gap/misconception — 'any dead animal becomes a fossil, bones just slowly turn into fossils': contrast the millions of animals that have died with the few fossils found, and make burial-before-decay the pivotal step using the rotting-in-the-open image.

Misconception — 'the real bones are still there, just very old and hard': introduce mineral replacement — over millions of years, minerals from groundwater soak in and the original material is often gradually swapped for rock minerals, so the fossil is usually stone in the shape of the bone rather than the unchanged bone.
Misconception — timescale collapse ('fossils form in a few years'): anchor the millions-of-years timescale with the sediment-turning-to-rock step; a buried bone next year is still just a buried bone.

Follow-up probes: 'Why don't we find fossils of most animals that ever lived?'; 'If you buried a chicken bone in your garden, would it be a fossil next year? Why not?' (treat as a relative, condition-dependent teaching device, not an absolute); 'What does the word sediment actually mean?'; 'Where do the minerals come from?'
activities.intendedInsight: Consolidate and check the sequence, the role of rapid burial, mineral replacement, and the rarity of fossils.
learnerActions: Put the stages in the correct order: dies → buried in sediment → minerals replace the remains → sediment hardens to rock → erosion exposes it.
Answer: why don't most animals that die become fossils?
Answer: what happens to the original hard parts over millions of years?

Respond to the diagnostic prompt: 'A dinosaur dies out in the open on dry ground and its body just lies there. Millions of years pass. Will there be a fossil of it? Say yes or no — and explain what has to happen for a fossil to form.'
